name: Complicated Urinary Tract Infection

pathogens.why: Complicating factors (catheters, structural abnormality, diabetes, male sex) select for a broader and more resistant organism profile than uncomplicated cystitis, including a meaningfully higher chance of ESBL-producing organisms.

investigations.why: Essential in complicated UTI given higher rates of resistant organisms - guides definitive therapy.
Assesses baseline renal function, particularly relevant if structural abnormality or obstruction is suspected.

investigations.test: Renal ultrasound (if recurrent or treatment failure)
investigations.why: Evaluates for obstruction, stones, or structural abnormality contributing to complicated infection.

clinicalPearls: Harrison defines complicated UTI as infection extending beyond the bladder (e.g., prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or UTI occurring in the setting of intermittent or indwelling catheterization; this is a shift from the older approach that automatically labeled any UTI in men, diabetics, the immunocompromised, or those with anatomic abnormalities as complicated (p.1129-1130).
Recurrent UTI is not inherently complicated; individual episodes may be uncomplicated and managed as such (p.1130).

Fever, rigors, and unilateral back or flank pain are incompatible with infection confined to the bladder and should trigger evaluation for infection beyond the bladder (kidney, prostate, or bloodstream) (p.1132).

In men, UTI is uncommon outside the context of catheterization/instrumentation or obstructive uropathy from prostatic hypertrophy; a urine culture should be obtained in every case of male UTI (p.1132).
Men with febrile UTI, even at first episode, should undergo imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, specifically to assess for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (p.1132).

Predictors of a surgically correctable disorder in men with febrile UTI include urinary retention symptoms, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties; men with none of these had normal urinary tracts on workup (p.1132).
Early recurrence within 2 weeks is regarded as relapse rather than reinfection and may signal a sequestered focus of ongoing infection that needs evaluation (p.1130).
Foreign bodies such as stones, stents, and catheters provide an inert surface for bacterial colonization and persistent biofilm formation, serving as a nidus for recurrent infection (p.1130-1131).
Initial evaluation of recurrent cystitis should include imaging to identify renal calculi or another nidus of infection and assessment for urinary retention (p.1138).
harrison.pathophysiology: Most UTIs arise by ascent of bacteria from the urethra to the bladder, with further ascent up the ureter producing renal parenchymal infection; the hematogenous route accounts for under 2% of cases and typically involves virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella (isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia). Whether bladder entry leads to symptomatic infection depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. Conditions causing urinary stasis or obstruction (vesicoureteral reflux, ureteral obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy, neurogenic bladder, urinary-diversion surgery) and foreign bodies that support biofilm all predispose to infection. Uropathogenic E. coli virulence factors include P fimbriae (mediating binding to renal epithelial receptors and important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion) and type 1 pili (mediating mannose binding and initiating bladder infection), plus toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilm formation, and capsules. Candiduria is pathogenetically distinct in that the hematogenous route is more common, and in non-instrumented immunocompetent patients its presence implies either genital contamination or possible widespread visceral dissemination (p.1131).
additionalDifferentials: Acute bacterial prostatitis (consider in men with UTI plus systemic symptoms and no other clear anatomic source) (p.1132)
Chronic bacterial prostatitis (consider with recurrent UTI in men, especially outside catheterization) (p.1132)
Pyelonephritis with or without urinary obstruction (p.1132-1133)
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (not associated with bacteriuria, not improved by antibiotics) (p.1132)
infectionMimics: Sexually transmitted infection / cervicitis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) presenting with dysuria (p.1133)
Urethritis from STI pathogens (gonococcal, chlamydial, Mycoplasma genitalium); urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt STI evaluation (p.1130, p.1133)
nonInfectiousMimics: Asymptomatic bacteriuria misclassified as UTI, especially in older patients with isolated altered mentation; degree of pyuria should not drive the distinction (p.1132)
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (p.1132)
additionalInvestigations: CT or ultrasound imaging in men with febrile UTI to evaluate for anatomic abnormality or obstruction (p.1132)
Blood cultures when complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, or systemic features are present (p.1134 diagnostic algorithm)
Urine dipstick (nitrite and leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tools mainly useful for ruling out UTI when the clinical diagnosis is unclear (p.1133-1135)
Imaging to identify renal calculi or other nidus, plus assessment for urinary retention, in recurrent UTI (p.1138)
Serum creatinine monitoring (a rapid rise may be the first sign of bilateral papillary necrosis) (p.1133)
redFlags: Fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, and flank pain suggesting severe pyelonephritis or infection beyond the bladder (p.1133)
Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy, suggesting intraparenchymal renal abscess (p.1133)
Failure to respond clinically within 72 h, prompting evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (p.1137)
Gas in renal/perinephric tissues (emphysematous pyelonephritis), almost exclusive to poorly controlled diabetes (p.1133)
Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter complicating pyelonephritis (p.1133)
Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine, raising concern for concomitant bacteremia / hematogenous seeding (p.1131)
Symptoms of urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, or voiding difficulty in men with febrile UTI (predict surgically correctable disease) (p.1132)
harrison.prognosis: Most simple cystitis carries a low risk of serious complication, but tissue-invasive complicated disease (pyelonephritis and beyond) carries greater risk and patients are often systemically ill. Pyelonephritis may be complicated by acute papillary necrosis with obstruction (requiring relief of obstruction to preserve renal function), perinephric or renal cortical abscess (often requiring percutaneous drainage), emphysematous pyelonephritis (a severe form, almost exclusive to poorly controlled diabetes), and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (suppurative renal destruction associated with chronic obstruction, often by staghorn calculi, that can mimic renal malignancy and frequently requires nephrectomy). Bilateral papillary necrosis is rare but may present with a rapid rise in creatinine (p.1133, p.1137).
pitfalls: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings: it does not reduce future UTI and may even increase risk, possibly by promoting colonization with more virulent/resistant pathogens (p.1129, p.1136).

Ending the workup of a febrile catheterized patient at an abnormal urinalysis: bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable with catheterization, so other infectious and noninfectious causes must be systematically excluded before diagnosing CAUTI (p.1133-1134).
Premature diagnostic closure in elderly patients with isolated delirium; collateral history is needed and a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB (p.1132).
Relying on a negative urine dipstick to rule out bacteriuria in pregnancy; it is not sensitive enough and culture-based ASB screening is required (p.1135).

Using nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin as if they treat tissue-invasive disease; they do not achieve adequate renal tissue levels and should not be used for pyelonephritis, and nitrofurantoin is inactive against many Proteus, Providencia, Morganella, Pseudomonas, Serratia, and some Klebsiella/Enterobacter (knowledge of intrinsic resistance) (p.1136-1137).
Interpreting a mixed-flora urine culture as infection; it usually represents contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula (p.1135).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames the practical categorization around whether infection is confined to the bladder (uncomplicated cystitis) versus extends beyond it (complicated UTI: prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) and whether catheter-associated (CAUTI). The key bedside questions are whether the patient is stable for outpatient management, whether a recalcitrant/recurrent source (e.g., obstructing calculi) must be identified, and whether the chosen agent must reach adequate blood and renal-tissue levels in addition to urine. Pyelonephritis itself ranges from mild (low-grade fever +/- back or costovertebral angle pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain) (p.1130, p.1133).
